scenes.title: A Definition of Rhetoric
scenes.summary: Rhetoric is a capacity to see, in each case, the possible means of persuasion. Every other art teaches and persuades about its own subject, as medicine about health and geometry about magnitudes; rhetoric seems able to see what is persuasive about whatever is given.

scenes.title: Artistic and Non-Artistic Proofs
scenes.summary: Some proofs are there beforehand, such as witnesses, tortures and contracts, and have only to be used; others are built by the method and by the speaker, and have to be found.

scenes.title: Three Kinds of Proof
scenes.summary: Proofs furnished by the speech lie in the character of the speaker, in putting the hearer into a frame of mind, and in the argument itself. Character, made in the speech itself, is almost the most authoritative proof; the hearers judge differently when pained or glad; and the argument shows what is true or seems true.

scenes.title: An Offshoot of Dialectic and Ethics
scenes.summary: So the orator must be able to reason, and to understand characters, virtues and the emotions. Rhetoric is an offshoot of dialectic and of the study of characters, which is politics, and for that reason it, and those who claim it, put on the guise of politics; like dialectic it is a capacity for furnishing arguments, not a science.

scenes.title: Example and Enthymeme
scenes.summary: As dialectic has induction, syllogism and the apparent syllogism, rhetoric has the example, the enthymeme and the apparent enthymeme: the example is rhetorical induction, the enthymeme rhetorical syllogism, and every proof by showing uses one or the other. Speeches full of examples persuade no less, but enthymemes win more applause.

scenes.title: For Simple Hearers
scenes.summary: Like dialectic, rhetoric studies not what seems so to an individual but to kinds of people, and what people already deliberate about: things that can be otherwise, before hearers who cannot follow long chains of argument. So the enthymeme uses few premises, leaving out what everyone knows: that Dorieus won at Olympia is enough, without adding that the prize is a crown.

scenes.title: Probabilities and Signs
scenes.summary: Since few premises are necessary, enthymemes are drawn from probabilities, what happens for the most part, and from signs. Some signs stand as particular to universal (Socrates was wise and just), some as universal to particular (fast breathing, fever); the necessary sign alone, as milk shows a birth, is a tekmērion, a word that once meant limit.

scenes.title: The Example of the Bodyguard
scenes.summary: The example argues neither from part to whole nor from whole to part, but from like to like under a common class: Dionysius asks for a bodyguard and must be aiming at tyranny, as Pisistratus and Theagenes of Megara did before him.

scenes.title: Common and Special Topics
scenes.summary: The greatest and least noticed difference among enthymemes: some use the common topics, like more and less, which apply to justice, nature and politics alike, others the special premises of each science; the better one chooses special premises, the more one leaves rhetoric for another science. Most enthymemes use the special premises, and the kinds of rhetoric must be determined first.
